summary: Describes ingress traffic filtering, a simple method to stop denial of service attacks that use forged source IP addresses from spreading out of behind an ISP's aggregation point. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: A mailroom checks that the return address on each outgoing letter belongs to your building. This asks network providers to do the same, so attackers cannot pretend to be someone else.

subtitle: Why providers should drop outgoing packets whose source addresses do not belong to the network they came from.

tldr.problem: Attackers launching denial of service floods can forge the source IP address on their packets, which hides who they are and can hurt innocent third parties.
tldr.mechanism: An ISP filters traffic on the ingress link from a customer network and only forwards packets whose source addresses fall within the prefixes legitimately advertised for that network.
tldr.outcome: Forged-source attacks from behind the filter are blocked and the true origin is easier to trace, though attackers can still spoof other addresses inside the permitted range.

facts.label: Filter action
facts.value: Deny packets with other source addresses

today: RFC 2827 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 38) and has been updated by RFC 3704. It obsoleted RFC 2267.

sections.title: The Spoofing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2827 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 2267. It responds to a resurgence of denial of service (DoS) attacks that use forged source addresses. The RFC urges all providers of Internet connectivity to filter so that attackers cannot use source addresses that do not sit within legitimately advertised prefixes.

The RFC is upfront about limits. The filtering does nothing against flooding attacks that originate from valid prefixes. It only stops an attacker inside the originating network from using forged addresses that break the filtering rules.

A side benefit is traceability: since the attacker must use a valid and reachable source address, the originator can be traced to its true source more easily.
sections.eli5: Bad guys can write a fake return address on their mail. This document asks the post offices to catch the fakes before the mail leaves.

sections.title: How Forged-Source Floods Work
sections.content:
The RFC's main example is a TCP SYN flood. An attacker inside the prefix 204.69.207.0/24 sends connection requests to a target host using randomly changing source addresses, such as ones from private ranges that are not in global routing tables. The target replies with SYN/ACK packets that go nowhere, but it reserves resources while it waits. Because the attacker changes the bogus address on each packet, more host resources are exhausted.

A second case uses someone else's valid address. The target then sends many SYN/ACK packets to that innocent system, so two systems are abused at once. The administrator under attack may also filter all traffic from the apparent source, which denies service to legitimate end systems and makes the administrator an unwitting accomplice.

The RFC also mentions similar attacks with UDP and ICMP flooding. It says administrators should never allow UDP packets for system diagnostic ports from outside their administrative domain, and that border routers should not forward directed broadcast packets by default. The result of these attacks is degraded performance or a system crash.

Operating system vendors had modified their software so servers can withstand very high connection attempt rates. The RFC calls this welcome and necessary, and expects it to work together with ingress filtering, which will take time to deploy everywhere.
sections.eli5: A sneaky kid sends lots of knocks on your door, each signed with a different made-up name, so you keep waiting for people who do not exist. Or he signs a real neighbor's name, and the neighbor gets blamed.

sections.title: Ingress Filtering at the Provider Edge
sections.content:
The core idea is to restrict transit traffic from a downstream network to the known, intentionally advertised prefixes. In the RFC's example, the attacker sits in 204.69.207.0/24, which gets connectivity from ISP D through router 2. An input filter on the ingress link of router 2 allows only traffic with source addresses within that prefix.

The filter logic is simple: if the source address is within 204.69.207.0/24, forward as appropriate; if it is anything else, deny the packet. Network administrators should log the dropped packets, which gives a basis for monitoring suspicious activity.

In general, an ISP that aggregates routing announcements for several downstream networks should strictly filter out traffic claiming to originate outside those announcements.
sections.eli5: The guard at the edge of your street checks that each outgoing letter says it comes from a house on your street. Letters with any other return address are thrown away, and the guard writes down what was thrown away.

sections.title: Further Capabilities and Rejected Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that future platforms could do automatic filtering on remote access servers. A user dialing in is usually one PC, and the only valid source address for it is the one assigned by the ISP, whether static or dynamic. The server could check every packet on ingress. Provisions are needed when a customer legitimately attaches a net or subnet through a remote router, so this could be an optional parameter.

The authors considered suggesting that routers also check that the return path to the source address leaves by the same interface the packet arrived on, as suggested in RFC 1812. They rejected it because of the number of asymmetric routes in the Internet, which would make it problematic.
sections.eli5: For someone dialing in from home, the provider knows exactly which return address that person has been given, so it can check each letter. A fancier check was dropped because mail often comes back by a different road than it went out on.

sections.title: Liabilities and Side Effects
sections.content:
Ingress filtering can break some special services, so ISPs offering them should consider alternative methods. Mobile IP is specifically affected: traffic to the mobile node is tunneled but traffic from it is not, so its packets carry source addresses that do not match the network it is attached to. The Mobile IP Working Group developed reverse tunnels (RFC 2344), which send the mobile node's traffic through a tunnel to the home agent first. Implementers of mobile IP are encouraged to use them.

Ingress filtering does not stop an attacker from forging the address of another host inside the permitted prefix range. It does guarantee that the attack comes from within the known advertised prefixes, so the culprit is easier to find, and at worst the administrator can block a range of source addresses.

Where DHCP or BOOTP is used, administrators should ensure that packets from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 can reach the relay agent in routers when appropriate, while keeping directed broadcast replication under control.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a traveler really does send mail from a different place than home, and the guard might stop it. Special routes were invented so the traveler's mail goes home first and then out with a correct return address.

sections.title: Recommendations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The summary recommends that all service providers filter at the periphery of Internet-connected networks as soon as possible. A provider that can demonstrate it already filters on customer links can also help locate the source of an attack. Corporate administrators should filter so their own networks are not the source of such problems. Filtering could also catch users who improperly attach systems to the wrong networks, and block a disgruntled employee from anonymous attacks.

The RFC's security considerations state that its intent is to increase security practices and awareness. As more providers and corporate administrators filter, attackers have fewer opportunities to use forged source addresses, and tracking the source of the remaining attacks becomes simpler because the source is more likely to be valid.
sections.eli5: Everyone who runs a post office should check return addresses, and big companies should check their own mail too. That makes it harder to hide and easier to catch whoever is sending the trouble.

data.title: Ingress filter
data.code:
IF    packet's source address from within 204.69.207.0/24
THEN  forward as appropriate

IF    packet's source address is anything else
THEN  deny packet
